warmup.q: A month-end report runs SELECT sum(balance_cents) FROM wallets for 30 seconds under REPEATABLE READ. Meanwhile 5,000 transfers update rows of the same table and commit. What does the report see, and do the transfers wait for it?
options: It holds a read lock, so the transfers wait 30 seconds, and it sees the balances as they were at its start
Some transfers and not others, depending on how far its scan had got when each one committed
The balances as they were when it took its snapshot, and the transfers never wait for it
The transfers fail with a serialization error, because the report is reading their rows
warmup.why: Each transfer writes a new version of its rows and leaves the old versions in place. The report's snapshot tells it to keep reading the versions that had committed when it began, so it takes no lock and the writers never wait. The second option is what you get with neither locks nor versions: a sum that is off by every half-seen transfer. The first option is how databases worked before MVCC, and the last confuses this with write conflicts, which happen between two writers.

sections.h: Readers and writers stop waiting for each other when old versions stay
sections.html:
Lessons 1 to 3 leaned on one idea without opening it: a snapshot, a past moment that a transaction keeps reading while others write. This lesson opens it, starting from the problem it solves.

A settlement job sums the balances of 2 million wallets every evening, and the scan takes about 30 seconds. During those 30 seconds the payment service commits about 300 transfers a second, each one moving money between two wallets. A transfer creates no money and destroys none, so the sum must come out right to the cent however many transfers run during the scan.

Version 1 makes readers and writers take turns. The report locks the table for reading, and a transfer that wants to write waits until the report is done. The sum is right, and about 9,000 transfers sit in a queue for 30 seconds. Your payment API times out instead.

Version 2 drops the lock. The report reads whatever each row holds when the scan gets there. Now a transfer moves 250 euros from wallet 7 to wallet 1,800,000 while the scan is halfway. The report read wallet 7 before the debit and reaches wallet 1,800,000 after the credit, so the sum is 250 euros too high. The next run is wrong by a different amount.

Version 3 keeps the old value. A transfer doesn't overwrite wallet 7. It writes a new version of the row and marks the old one "replaced by transaction 860". The report remembers which transactions had committed when it started, and for every row it reads the version that was current at that moment. The transfers never wait for the report, the report never waits for the transfers, and the sum is exact. This is multi-version concurrency control (MVCC). PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL's InnoDB all work this way. They differ in where they keep the old versions, and the last section compares them.

The Storage engines track's lesson on pages, tuples and heap files showed where PostgreSQL keeps the marks: in every tuple header (a tuple is one stored version of a row). t_xmin is the id of the transaction that created this version, and t_xmax the id of the one that deleted or replaced it, 0 while nobody has. A transaction id (xid) is a 32-bit counter: each transaction that writes takes the next number. An UPDATE is a delete plus an insert. It sets t_xmax on the old version, writes a complete new version with its own id in t_xmin, and points the old version's t_ctid at the new one, so the versions of one row form a chain. In the Try it, updating wallet 2 leaves slot 2 where it was, with t_xmax = 858, and puts the new balance in slot 4.

The figure is the picture for this lesson: a chain of versions, each stamped with who created it and who ended it, and readers that each pick one version. The rest of the lesson answers four questions about it. How does a reader pick? What happens when two writers want the same row? Who throws the old versions away? And how do other engines keep them?

try.title: See both versions of an updated row
steps: From labs/, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait and open psql with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.
Create a small wallets table and look at its rows with the hidden xmin and xmax columns.
Update wallet 2. Predict: how many tuples does page 0 hold now, and what is in slot 2's t_xmax? Then read the page with pageinspect, which lists every tuple whether or not any snapshot can see it.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE wallets (id int PRIMARY KEY, balance_cents bigint) WITH (autovacuum_enabled = off); INSERT INTO wallets VALUES (1, 50000), (2, 50000), (3, 50000); SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM wallets; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 2500 WHERE id = 2; SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM wallets; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0));

try.expect:
ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | balance_cents
-------+------+------+----+---------------
 (0,1) |  857 |    0 |  1 |         50000
 (0,2) |  857 |    0 |  2 |         50000
 (0,3) |  857 |    0 |  3 |         50000

 ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | balance_cents
-------+------+------+----+---------------
 (0,1) |  857 |    0 |  1 |         50000
 (0,3) |  857 |    0 |  3 |         50000
 (0,4) |  858 |    0 |  2 |         47500

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------
  1 |    857 |      0 | (0,1)
  2 |    857 |    858 | (0,4)
  3 |    857 |      0 | (0,3)
  4 |    858 |      0 | (0,4)

xmin and xmax are system columns every table has; SELECT * hides them. After the UPDATE, a query sees wallet 2 only at (0,4), written by transaction 858. The page still holds the old version in slot 2, stamped t_xmax = 858, with t_ctid pointing at slot 4: four tuples for three rows. Your ids differ. Turning autovacuum off for this table keeps the background cleanup of the last section from tidying the page before you look.

sections.h: A snapshot says which transactions you can see
sections.html:
A reader needs a rule that picks exactly one version of every row. The first idea is a timestamp: "show me each row as it was at 18:00:00.000". That needs the commit time of every transaction, and transaction ids are not handed out in commit order. In the Try it, transfer 859 starts first and commits last, while wallet 4's insert, id 860, starts later and commits first.

PostgreSQL's answer is a snapshot: a short list of which transactions count as finished for this reader. SELECT pg_current_snapshot() prints it in three parts, like 859:861:859:

  • xmin (859): every id below it had finished when the snapshot was taken.
  • xmax (861): one past the newest transaction that had finished. No id from here up had finished, so none of them counts.
  • the list after the second colon: ids in between that were still running (here 859, the open transfer).

So the snapshot sees a transaction's changes if it committed, is below xmax and is not on the running list. Your own changes you always see. Put that together with the two stamps and you have the visibility rule: a version is visible if the snapshot sees its xmin, and its xmax is 0 or not seen. Wallet 1's old version, xmin 857, xmax 859, is visible to 859:861:859: 857 committed long ago, and 859 was running. The new version, xmin 859, is not. So the report reads 50,000, and it keeps reading 50,000 after 859 commits, because 859 sits on its list for good. Wallet 4, xmin 860, is visible, even though 860 started after the transfer.

"Did it commit?" is the one question the snapshot can't answer. PostgreSQL keeps the answer in the commit log (pg_xact): two bits per transaction id, for in progress, committed or aborted. COMMIT makes its WAL record durable (the Storage engines track's write-ahead logging lesson), then sets its own two bits. It doesn't touch a single row, which is why committing one row costs the same as committing a million. Looking up the commit log for every tuple would be slow, so the first reader to learn the answer writes it into the tuple header as a hint bit, and later readers skip the lookup. An aborted transaction needs no undo either: its bits say aborted, so its versions fail the rule for every snapshot.

When does a transaction take its snapshot? That is what the isolation level decides. Under READ COMMITTED, PostgreSQL's default, every statement takes a new snapshot, so each statement sees everything committed before it began. Under REPEATABLE READ, the first statement takes the snapshot and the transaction keeps it to the end. Lesson 1 showed what each level lets an application see; underneath, the difference is only when the snapshot is taken. One more detail: a transaction gets an id only when it first writes. A read-only transaction never uses one up.

try.title: Watch a snapshot keep an old balance
steps: Open a second terminal in labs/ and run the same psql command there. Keep both side by side: terminal 1 and terminal 2 below.

In terminal 1, start a transfer on wallet 1 and leave it open. In terminal 2, insert wallet 4, then start a REPEATABLE READ report, print its snapshot and read all wallets. Predict the three parts of the snapshot, and whether the report sees wallet 4.
Commit in terminal 1. In terminal 2, read again and look at the page. Predict the report's answer for wallet 1. Then commit in terminal 2 and read once more.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: a slow transfer, left open BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 1000 WHERE id = 1; SELECT pg_current_xact_id() AS writer; -- terminal 2: a new customer's wallet, then a report INSERT INTO wallets VALUES (4, 50000); BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT pg_current_snapshot(); SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id; -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2 SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0)); COMMIT; SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id;

try.expect:
Terminal 1 prints writer = 859. Terminal 2:

 pg_current_snapshot
---------------------
 859:861:859

 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         50000
  2 |         47500
  3 |         50000
  4 |         50000

After terminal 1 commits, the report's query returns exactly the same four rows, while the page holds both versions of wallet 1:

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------
  1 |    857 |    859 | (0,5)
  2 |    857 |    858 | (0,4)
  3 |    857 |      0 | (0,3)
  4 |    858 |      0 | (0,4)
  5 |    859 |      0 | (0,5)
  6 |    860 |      0 | (0,6)

After its own COMMIT, terminal 2 reads wallet 1 as 49,000. The snapshot lists 859 as running, so the report keeps slot 1 (its deleter 859 is on the list) and skips slot 5 (its creator 859 is on the list), even after 859 commits. Wallet 4 in slot 6 was inserted by 860, which started after the transfer but committed before the snapshot, and the report sees it. Your ids differ.

sections.h: Two writers on one row: the second waits, then decides
sections.html:
Snapshots let readers ignore writers. Two writers can't ignore each other. Transfer A takes 700 from wallet 3 while refund B adds 100 to it, at the same moment, and both read 50,000. If each wrote a new version on top of the one it read, wallet 3 would have two current versions, 49,300 and 50,100, and one of the two changes would be lost. This is lesson 2's lost update.

So a writer has to check the version it is about to replace, and in PostgreSQL that check sits in the version's t_xmax. When A updates wallet 3, it writes its id into the old version's t_xmax. That number is the row lock: "transaction 861 is replacing this version". When B reaches the same version and finds a t_xmax that belongs to a transaction still in progress, it doesn't overwrite it. It waits for A to end. PostgreSQL keeps no table of row locks in memory, which could run out with millions of rows locked; the docs say it remembers nothing about modified rows in memory. The lock is in the row, and B waits on A's transaction id. Lesson 5 watches that wait in pg_locks.

When A ends, B decides what to do next, and its isolation level decides for it:

  • A aborted: its t_xmax means nothing. B updates the version it found.
  • A committed and B runs READ COMMITTED: B follows the old version's t_ctid to A's new version, checks its WHERE clause again on that version, and applies its change there. 49,300 + 100 = 49,400, and nothing is lost.
  • A committed and B runs REPEATABLE READ: B can't do that. Its snapshot says A's version doesn't exist, and changing a version you can't see would break the snapshot. PostgreSQL aborts B with could not serialize access due to concurrent update, SQLSTATE 40001, and the application must retry the whole transaction.

This rule is called first-updater-wins: the first transaction to stamp t_xmax gets the row, and the second waits to learn whether it may go on. Your lab store can't wait yet, so it fails the second writer at once with WriteConflict when someone it can't see has touched the row and hasn't aborted. Lesson 5 builds the waiting.

So "readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers" is true, and it's only half the story. Writers still block writers.

try.title: Make a second writer wait, then fail
steps: Terminal 1: start transfer A on wallet 3 and leave it open.
Terminal 2: start a REPEATABLE READ transaction, read wallet 3, look at slot 3's stamps, then update wallet 3. Predict: does the UPDATE return?
Commit in terminal 1 and watch terminal 2. Roll terminal 2 back. Then run the same race with READ COMMITTED in terminal 2 and predict the balance it returns.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: transfer A, left open BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 700 WHERE id = 3; -- terminal 2: refund B under REPEATABLE READ BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT balance_cents FROM wallets WHERE id = 3; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0)) WHERE lp = 3; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 100 WHERE id = 3; -- waits -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2: the UPDATE has failed; end the transaction ROLLBACK; -- the same race with READ COMMITTED, the default, in terminal 2 -- terminal 1 BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 700 WHERE id = 3; -- terminal 2 BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 100 WHERE id = 3 RETURNING balance_cents; -- waits -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2 COMMIT;

try.expect:
The refund reads 50,000, and slot 3 already carries A's id in t_xmax, though A hasn't committed:

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+--------+--------
  3 |    857 |    861

The REPEATABLE READ UPDATE hangs. The moment terminal 1 commits, it fails:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update

In the READ COMMITTED round the UPDATE also hangs, then succeeds when terminal 1 commits, on top of A's new version:

 balance_cents
---------------
         48700

50,000 minus two transfers of 700 is 48,600, plus the refund's 100 is 48,700: nothing was lost. Your ids differ.

sections.h: VACUUM removes what no snapshot can see, and freezes what everyone can
sections.html:
Every UPDATE leaves the old version behind. In the Try it, 10,000 settlement rows updated twice leave 20,000 dead versions, and the table grows from 55 pages to 163. Something has to clean up, and it must know when a version is safe to remove.

A version is safe to remove when no snapshot can ever see it again: the transaction in its xmax committed, and every snapshot still in use was taken after that. PostgreSQL tracks this with one number, the horizon: the lowest xmin of any snapshot in use, or of any transaction still running. Every transaction below the horizon had finished before any of those snapshots was taken. So a version whose xmax committed below the horizon is invisible to every snapshot, now and later, and VACUUM may remove it. A version created by an aborted transaction can go at once.

One number for the whole database makes a long transaction expensive. In the Try it, one REPEATABLE READ report stays open while the updates run, and VACUUM reports 20000 are dead but not yet removable. The report can't see those versions either: they were created and deleted after its snapshot. But VACUUM only compares with the horizon, so it keeps them. When the report commits, the same VACUUM removes all 20,000. The usual culprits are a REPEATABLE READ transaction left open, a transaction that wrote something and then sat idle in transaction, and a replica that reports its oldest query back to the primary (hot_standby_feedback). A READ COMMITTED transaction that has only read holds the horizon only while a statement runs.

Removing a dead version works the way the heap-file lesson of the Storage engines track showed for a DELETE: VACUUM removes the index entries that point at it, marks its slot unused, compacts the page and notes the free space. It doesn't shrink the file. The table is still 163 pages afterwards, and the free space holds the next updates. A query that reads a nearly full page also prunes dead versions on the spot, without waiting for VACUUM. If an update changed no indexed column and its new version fit on the same page, it was a HOT update (heap-only tuple): no new index entry was written, and pruning leaves the old slot as a redirect to the new one, so the index still finds the row.

VACUUM's second job concerns the ids. They are 32-bit and compared in a circle: for any id, the 2 billion before it count as the past and the 2 billion after it as the future. A payments database that commits 2,000 write transactions a second uses 2 billion ids in under 12 days. A version written 2 billion transactions ago would then look like it came from the future and vanish. So VACUUM freezes old versions: it marks them "committed, visible to every snapshot", and nobody reads their xmin again. Autovacuum forces a freezing pass on any table whose oldest unfrozen id is more than 200 million transactions old (autovacuum_freeze_max_age). If freezing can't keep up, PostgreSQL warns 40 million ids before the limit, and 3 million before it, it refuses to start any transaction that would need a new id. The stepper follows one row from UPDATE to freezing.

frames.say: R commits, and with nothing else running the horizon moves up to 861. Slot 1's deleter 860 is below it and committed, so every snapshot from now on sees slot 1 as deleted. VACUUM removes it and the space is free for the next version. Because this was a HOT update (no indexed column changed), slot 1 stays as a redirect to slot 2, and the primary-key entry that points at slot 1 still finds wallet 7.

frames.say: Months later the counter has moved on by hundreds of millions. Ids are 32-bit and compared in a circle, so in about 2 billion more transactions 860 would look like an id from the future and slot 2 would vanish. Before that, VACUUM freezes slot 2: it sets a flag that says "committed, visible to everyone". From then on nobody looks at its xmin again.

try.title: Hold VACUUM back with one open report
steps: Terminal 1: open a REPEATABLE READ report and run one query, which takes its snapshot. Leave it open.
Terminal 2: create settlements, update every row twice, check the size and the dead-version count, and run VACUUM (VERBOSE). Predict how many dead versions it removes.
Commit terminal 1 and vacuum again. Then compare the table's age(relfrozenxid) before and after VACUUM (FREEZE).

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: a report that stays open BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT sum(balance_cents) FROM wallets; -- terminal 2: make 20,000 dead versions, then vacuum CREATE TABLE settlements (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents bigint) WITH (autovacuum_enabled = off); INSERT INTO settlements SELECT g, 1000 FROM generate_series(1, 10000) g; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1; UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT pg_stat_force_next_flush(); SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'settlements'; VACUUM (VERBOSE) settlements; -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2: vacuum again, then freeze VACUUM (VERBOSE) settlements; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT count(DISTINCT (ctid::text::point)[0]) AS pages_with_rows FROM settlements; SELECT age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'settlements'; VACUUM (FREEZE) settlements; SELECT age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'settlements'; SELECT t_xmin, combined_flags FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('settlements', 162)), LATERAL heap_tuple_infomask_flags(t_infomask, t_infomask2) WHERE lp_flags = 1 LIMIT 1; SHOW autovacuum_freeze_max_age;

try.expect:
The table grows from 55 pages to 163, and the statistics count the dead versions (pg_stat_force_next_flush() makes the counters current at once):

 n_live_tup | n_dead_tup
------------+------------
      10000 |      20000

The first VACUUM, with the report open, removes nothing:

tuples: 0 removed, 30000 remain, 20000 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 873, which was 4 XIDs old when operation ended

After the report commits:

tuples: 20000 removed, 10000 remain, 0 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 879, which was 4 XIDs old when operation ended
visibility map: 163 pages set all-visible, 108 pages set all-frozen (0 were all-visible)

(output trimmed). removable cutoff is the horizon. The file is still 163 pages, but only 55 of them hold rows: the other 108 are empty and ready for the next updates, which is also why VACUUM could mark 108 pages all-frozen. Then the freeze: age(relfrozenxid) goes from 8 to 0, and a live tuple keeps its t_xmin but is flagged frozen:

 t_xmin |   combined_flags
--------+--------------------
    876 | {HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN}

 autovacuum_freeze_max_age
---------------------------
 200000000

age(relfrozenxid) counts how many transactions old the table's oldest unfrozen id is. Your ids differ. When you are done with this lesson, drop the two tables (DROP TABLE wallets, settlements;) or delete the whole database with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Routine vacuuming (dead tuples, freezing, wraparound)
Pavlo and Zhang: The part of PostgreSQL we hate the most

sections.h: Where the old versions live: PostgreSQL's heap, InnoDB's undo log, Oracle's undo segments
sections.html:
Every MVCC engine keeps old versions for old snapshots. Where it keeps them decides who pays for them, and what a long-open transaction breaks.

PostgreSQL keeps every version in the table itself, oldest first, each a complete copy of the row. An old snapshot reads its version directly. Everyone else pays: scans step over dead versions, an update that isn't HOT adds entries to every index, and VACUUM must visit the table and its indexes to clean up.

InnoDB, MySQL's engine, updates the row in place in its clustered index, the B+tree that holds the table's rows in primary-key order. Before it overwrites the row, it writes the old values of the changed columns to an undo log. Each row has two hidden columns for this: DB_TRX_ID, the last transaction that wrote it, and DB_ROLL_PTR, a pointer to the undo record with the values before that write. A reader whose snapshot is older than the row follows the pointers back through the undo records and rebuilds the version it should see. The table stays compact, and the old reader pays: the older its snapshot, the longer the chain it walks. A purge thread throws away undo records once no snapshot can need them, InnoDB's VACUUM.

Oracle works like InnoDB. It changes blocks in place, keeps the old images in undo segments, and rebuilds a block as of the moment a query started (or, at SERIALIZABLE, the transaction) when it reads. It keeps undo for a retention period and reuses the space after that. A long query that needs undo already overwritten fails with ORA-01555, snapshot too old.

So one long-open transaction hurts each engine in a different place:

PostgreSQL InnoDB Oracle
old versions live in the table and its indexes the undo log undo segments
a long transaction holds back VACUUM in every table holds back purge may lose the undo it needs
the symptom bloat: tables and indexes grow the history list and the undo log grow ORA-01555 for the long query

PostgreSQL's damage outlives the transaction. Once a table has grown, plain VACUUM makes the space reusable inside the file but doesn't give it back, so a table bloated by a session left idle in transaction all weekend stays large until it is rewritten. In InnoDB, the Try it holds one snapshot open while a thousand small updates commit. The history list length, InnoDB's count of committed transactions whose undo purge hasn't discarded yet, climbs to about a thousand and stays there until the snapshot closes. The MySQL docs warn that this happens even when the long transaction only reads.

try.title: Hold back InnoDB's purge with one open snapshot
steps: From the labs folder, start MySQL 8.4: docker compose -f env/mysql.yml up -d --wait. Its settlements table has 10,000 rows of 1,000 cents each. Open two terminals there.
Terminal 1: run docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course, start a transaction with a consistent snapshot and read the total. Leave it open.

Terminal 2: run 1,000 single-row updates, each its own transaction, then read InnoDB's history list length and the total. Predict both, and what terminal 1's next read returns. Then commit terminal 1 and check the history list again for half a minute. Stop MySQL afterwards: docker compose -f env/mysql.yml down -v.

code.title: two terminals in the labs folder
code.html: # terminal 1, inside mysql START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT; SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements; # terminal 2: 1,000 transactions, one UPDATE each for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo "UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1 WHERE id = $i;" done | docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec -T db mysql course docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course -e " SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len'; SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements;" # terminal 1 SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements; COMMIT; # terminal 2, a few times over the next 30 seconds docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course -e " SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';"

try.expect:
Terminal 1's first read shows 10000000. After the updates, terminal 2 sees (output trimmed):

+----------------------+-------+
| name                 | count |
+----------------------+-------+
| trx_rseg_history_len |  1001 |
+----------------------+-------+
+----------+
| total    |
+----------+
| 10001000 |
+----------+

Terminal 1 still reads 10000000: InnoDB rebuilds its old versions from the undo records that purge isn't allowed to discard. After terminal 1 commits, the count stays at 1001 for a few seconds and then drops to 0 as purge catches up (within about 20 seconds here). Run the 1,000 updates again with no snapshot open and the count stays in single digits throughout: purge keeps up as long as nothing holds it back.

analogy: MVCC works like a JVM heap of immutable objects. An update never changes an object: it allocates a new one and moves the shared reference to it. A snapshot is a thread that still holds the old reference, so it keeps reading the old state for as long as it holds on, and nobody had to lock anything. VACUUM is the garbage collector, and an open transaction is a leaked GC root that keeps everything it can reach alive. The analogy breaks at reachability. A garbage collector traces real references and frees anything unreachable. VACUUM compares ids with one horizon, so an old snapshot also keeps alive versions it could never have seen, as long as they died after it started.
world: Oracle at work keeps its old versions in undo, so a long report there risks ORA-01555 rather than bloating the tables, and the DBA's undo retention setting is the knob. On PostgreSQL the same mistake costs everyone: a Quarkus @Transactional method that updates an authorization and then calls a card issuer, or waits on a Temporal activity, keeps its transaction id alive for as long as the call takes, and every table in the database keeps its dead versions for that long. Commit before the remote call, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a forgotten session ends itself, and alert on the oldest xact_start in pg_stat_activity. A Kafka consumer that writes a batch per transaction is fine; one that holds a transaction open across its whole poll loop is not. The same rule holds on MySQL, where the symptom is a growing history list.
mistake: The common mistake is treating VACUUM as a disk-space chore you can switch off or put off. Someone disables autovacuum on a hot ledger table because it uses I/O at peak, or a session sits idle in transaction for a day. Dead versions pile up: every scan reads through them, every non-HOT update adds index entries, and queries slow down with no change in the data. Left long enough, the oldest unfrozen id approaches the wraparound limit, autovacuum forces an aggressive freezing pass at the worst moment, and in the end the server stops assigning transaction ids. Leave autovacuum on and tune it per table instead: for a big, busy table, lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor from its 20% default so cleanup starts sooner. Alert on long transactions and on age(datfrozenxid).

compare.title: Where the old version lives: PostgreSQL vs InnoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL
a.title: versions in the table
a.html:
UPDATE wallet 7 SET balance = 250.00

heap page:
  slot 1  500.00  xmin 850  xmax 860  -> slot 2
  slot 2  250.00  xmin 860  xmax 0

old version: a whole copy of the row,
  in the table, oldest first
old snapshot: reads slot 1 directly
new index entry: only if not HOT
cleanup: VACUUM, of table and indexes

b.label: MySQL InnoDB
b.title: newest in place, old values in undo
b.html:
UPDATE wallet 7 SET balance = 250.00

clustered index leaf:
  wallet 7  250.00  DB_TRX_ID 860
            DB_ROLL_PTR -> undo record
undo log:
  wallet 7  balance was 500.00

old version: only the changed columns,
  in the undo log, newest first
old snapshot: rebuilds 500.00 from undo
new index entry: only if a key changed
cleanup: purge, of the undo log

compare.note: Both keep old versions for old snapshots; they differ in who pays. PostgreSQL copies the whole row on every update and leaves the old copy in the table, so scans step over dead versions until VACUUM runs, and an update that isn't HOT writes to every index. InnoDB changes the row in place and writes a small undo record, so the table stays compact; a reader with an old snapshot pays instead, walking undo records back from the newest version, and a long transaction makes the undo log grow and holds back purge. Oracle follows the InnoDB design.

steps.say: Wallet 7 has three versions. The commit log says 850 and 860 committed, and 875 aborted. Three readers took their snapshots at different times.
steps.code:
slot 1  500.00  xmin 850  xmax 860
slot 2  250.00  xmin 860  xmax 875
slot 3  100.00  xmin 875  xmax 0

S1 = 860:861:860     taken while 860 ran
S2 = 875:876:875     taken while 875 ran
S3 = 880:880:        taken after 875 aborted

steps.say: S1. Slot 1: 850 is below xmin 860 and committed, so its creator is seen; its deleter 860 is on the running list, so not seen. Slot 1 is visible: S1 reads 500.00. Slots 2 and 3 were created by 860 and 875, which S1 can't see.
steps.code: fun sees(s: Snapshot, xid: Long) = xid == s.owner || (xid < s.xmax && xid !in s.active && status(xid) == COMMITTED) sees(S1, 850) == true // slot 1's creator sees(S1, 860) == false // slot 1's deleter: on S1's running list

steps.say: S2. Slot 1's deleter 860 is below 875 and committed: slot 1 is deleted for S2. Slot 2: creator 860 seen, deleter 875 on the running list. S2 reads 250.00, and still would after 875 finished.
steps.code: isVisible(slot1, S2) == false // 860 deleted it, and S2 sees 860 isVisible(slot2, S2) == true // 875 is running for S2

steps.say: S3. 875 aborted, so S3 doesn't see it, as creator or as deleter. Slot 3 is invisible, and slot 2 is visible again: an aborted xmax counts as no xmax. S3 reads 250.00. No undo ran; the commit log alone did it.
steps.code: isVisible(slot2, S3) == true // xmax 875 aborted: ignored isVisible(slot3, S3) == false // xmin 875 aborted

steps.say: Now VACUUM, while S1 is still open. The horizon is S1's xmin, 860. Slot 1's deleter 860 is not below 860, so slot 1 stays, and slot 2 is live. Slot 3 can go at once, because an aborted creator means no snapshot will ever see it.
steps.code:
horizon = 860
slot 1: xmax 860 committed, but 860 >= 860   -> keep
slot 2: xmax 875 aborted                     -> live, keep
slot 3: xmin 875 aborted                     -> remove

lab.title: Build a multi-version store with snapshots and VACUUM
steps: Read the class comment of MvccStore.kt and everything below its "provided" line: begin takes the snapshot, commit and abort only write the commit log, and horizon is the oldest snapshot xmin.
Run the tests once. All 13 fail.
Write sees and isVisible, the visibility rule, then get. The tests about snapshots, own writes and aborted transactions pass.

Write checkWritable, put and delete. The conflict tests pass, and so does the write-skew test: read it, because it passes only because your store allows the anomaly. Lesson 5 shows how SERIALIZABLE catches it.
Write vacuum and run the tests until all 13 pass.
hints: In sees, check xid >= snapshot.xmax and xid in snapshot.active before you ask the commit log. A transaction that committed after the snapshot was taken says COMMITTED in the log, and it must still be invisible.
Get the snapshot with statementSnapshot(tx) in get, put and delete, never tx.snapshot directly. That one call is the whole difference between READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ.

checkWritable needs one test for both cases of section 3: a writer you can't see either is still running (PostgreSQL would wait) or committed after your snapshot (REPEATABLE READ fails). Skip ids that aborted.

In vacuum, compare xmax < horizon(), strictly. A version whose xmax equals the horizon was deleted by a transaction that was running when the oldest snapshot was taken, so that snapshot may still need it.

drill.title: Write the visibility rule from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write sees(snapshot, xid) and isVisible(version, snapshot) for a snapshot of (owner, xmin, xmax, active) and a version of (xmin, xmax), given status(xid) from the commit log. Then say which check makes REPEATABLE READ repeatable.

answer.html: fun sees(s: Snapshot, xid: Long): Boolean { if (xid == s.owner) return true // my own changes if (xid >= s.xmax) return false // not finished when I took the snapshot if (xid in s.active) return false // running when I took it return status(xid) == TxStatus.COMMITTED // finished: visible only if it committed } fun isVisible(v: Version, s: Snapshot): Boolean = sees(s, v.xmin) && !(v.xmax != 0L && sees(s, v.xmax)) // The `xid in s.active` and `xid >= s.xmax` checks: a transaction that was running when the // snapshot was taken stays invisible after it commits, so reading again gives the same answer.

recap: An UPDATE in PostgreSQL writes a whole new version and stamps the old one's t_xmax. Readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers.
A snapshot is xmin:xmax:running list. A version is visible if the snapshot sees its xmin and its xmax is 0 or not seen. COMMIT only sets two bits in the commit log.
READ COMMITTED takes a snapshot for every statement; REPEATABLE READ takes one for the whole transaction.
Writers still lock: the row lock is the old version's t_xmax. A second writer waits, then under REPEATABLE READ fails with 40001 if the first one committed.
VACUUM removes versions whose deleter committed below the horizon, the oldest snapshot in use, so one long transaction holds back cleanup everywhere. The file doesn't shrink.
Transaction ids are 32-bit and wrap around. VACUUM freezes old versions, and autovacuum forces it at 200 million ids of age.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "PostgreSQL uses MVCC, so it never locks rows. That's why two refunds on the same payment can't block each other." Explain what really happens.
explain.answer: MVCC means readers don't need locks: a reader picks the version of each row that its snapshot can see, and writers never wait for readers. Writers still lock. An UPDATE stamps the old version's t_xmax with its transaction id, and that stamp is the row lock. A second refund that reaches the same version finds a t_xmax belonging to a transaction that is still running, and waits for it to end. If the first refund commits, the second one under READ COMMITTED re-reads the new version and applies its change on top; under REPEATABLE READ it fails with a serialization error and must be retried. So two refunds on one payment do block each other, one after the other, and that is what stops one of them from being lost.

deeper.html:
VACUUM's other two jobs. The routine-vacuuming docs list four reasons to vacuum. Two are in this lesson: reclaiming dead versions and preventing wraparound. The third is the visibility map, two bits per heap page saying "every tuple here is visible to everyone" and "every tuple here is frozen". An index-only scan answers a query from the index alone, but it may skip reading a heap page only if that page's all-visible bit is set, and only VACUUM sets it, so a table that is rarely vacuumed gets slow index-only scans. The fourth is statistics: VACUUM ANALYZE and autovacuum's analyze step refresh the numbers the planner relies on (the Storage engines track's lesson on query optimization).

The cost of keeping whole copies. Andy Pavlo and Bohan Zhang's post on PostgreSQL's MVCC gives an example of 10 million live tuples and 40 million dead ones: a 50 GB table holding 10 GB of live data. Their criticisms are the same trade-offs as the compare block: full-row copies, version chains ordered oldest to newest, every index touched by a non-HOT update, and autovacuum that is hard to tune. Leaving free space on each page with fillfactor (the heap-file lesson's Try it set it to 80) makes HOT updates more likely.

Multixacts. One t_xmax holds one id, but several transactions can lock the same row in share mode at once (SELECT ... FOR SHARE, or foreign-key checks). PostgreSQL then stores a multixact id in t_xmax, which points to a list of lockers. Multixact ids are 32-bit too and need their own freezing, which is why the docs speak of "multixact ID wraparound" as well.

Finding the transaction that holds things back. In PostgreSQL, SELECT pid, state, xact_start, backend_xmin FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC NULLS LAST lists sessions by how old a snapshot they hold. Two holders don't show up there: a replication slot's xmin in pg_replication_slots, and a prepared transaction in pg_prepared_xacts, which survives restarts and keeps its snapshot until someone commits or rolls it back (lesson 7 creates one on purpose). In MySQL, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS prints the history list length and the oldest active transactions.
